title: Cell: The Unit of Life
tagline: The cell theory, each organelle in turn, and the transport that crosses the membrane.

overview.intro: Cell biology is the foundation the rest of the course rests on, and it is examined with unusual consistency: state the cell theory, describe an organelle with its structure and function, compare prokaryotic with eukaryotic cells, or explain how a substance crosses the membrane. This chapter moves through the theory and the discovery of the cell, then each organelle in turn, then the prokaryote-eukaryote comparison, and finally the membrane and the transport processes that cross it, so that structure, function and mechanism are joined rather than listed separately.

facts.label: Cell theory
facts.value: All living organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of structure and function, and cells arise only from pre-existing cells.

facts.label: Prokaryote size
facts.value: Bacteria are typically 1 to 5 micrometres long, while a human red blood cell is about 7 micrometres across.

facts.label: Mitochondrion
facts.value: A double-membraned organelle with cristae increasing the surface area for the electron transport chain and ATP synthesis.

facts.label: Semipermeable membrane
facts.value: The lipid bilayer with proteins allows water through freely but holds back solutes — the basis of osmosis.

learningOutcomes: State the cell theory and credit the scientists who established it.
Describe the structure and function of each eukaryotic organelle.
Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells under standard headings.
Explain the fluid mosaic model of the membrane.
Distinguish diffusion, osmosis, active transport and bulk transport with examples.

learn.title: Cell theory and the discovery of the cell

blocks.text: The cell theory states three things that are worth quoting exactly in an examination. First, all living organisms are composed of one or more cells. Second, the cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life — the smallest unit that can be said to be alive on its own. Third, cells arise only from pre-existing cells by division, so that no new living matter is assembled spontaneously. The history behind these statements gives the theory its authority: Robert Hooke observed cork in 1665 and named the box-like spaces he saw cells after the rooms in a monastery; Anton van Leeuwenhoek in the 1670s with single-lens microscopes saw living protozoa and bacteria in pond water and scrapings from his own teeth; Matthias Schleiden in 1838 concluded that all plants are made of cells; Theodor Schwann in 1839 extended this to animals and stated that the cell is the unit of structure; and Rudolf Virchow in 1855 proclaimed that all cells come from pre-existing cells by division, closing the theory against spontaneous generation. Later work with the electron microscope added that cells contain organelles with defined membranes, and the study of cell division established what a unit of reproduction actually means. A cell itself is bounded by a plasma membrane, holds cytoplasm containing organelles, and carries genetic material — a single circular chromosome in prokaryotes, and a nucleus containing linear chromosomes in eukaryotes — with ribosomes for protein synthesis in both.

items: All living organisms are made of one or more cells.
The cell is the basic structural and functional unit of life.
Cells arise only from pre-existing cells by division.
Hooke named cells from cork in 1665; Leeuwenhoek observed living microorganisms soon after.
Schleiden and Schwann extended the cell theory to plants and animals in 1838 to 1839.
Virchow’s dictum omne cellula e cellula completed the theory in 1855.
A cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, organelles and genetic material with ribosomes.

items.note: Hooke saw the empty boxes left when living contents had died and decayed, which is why he saw walls but no organelles.
A single-celled amoeba carries out nutrition, excretion, response and reproduction by itself, showing that the cell is a complete functional unit.

blocks.text: The eukaryotic cell is a compartmentalised factory, and each organelle is best understood by asking what it does and how its structure enables it. The nucleus, bounded by a double nuclear envelope perforated by pores, contains the chromosomes as chromatin with their DNA, and inside lies the nucleolus, a dense region where ribosomal RNA is transcribed and ribosome subunits are assembled; the pores let messenger RNA leave and proteins enter, so the nucleus directs the cell while remaining physically separate from the cytoplasm. Ribosomes, made of ribosomal RNA and protein and consisting of a large and a small subunit, are the sites of translation, where the message carried by messenger RNA is read into a polypeptide; they lie free in the cytoplasm or attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. The rough endoplasmic reticulum, a network of flattened membranous sacs studded with ribosomes, synthesises proteins destined for secretion, for the membrane or for lysosomes. The smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and handles lipid synthesis, carbohydrate metabolism and the detoxification of drugs and poisons. The Golgi apparatus, a stack of curved membranous cisternae with a cis receiving face and a trans shipping face, receives proteins from the endoplasmic reticulum, modifies them — adding carbohydrate to make glycoproteins, for example — sorts them, and packages them into secretory vesicles that fuse with the membrane to release their contents by exocytosis; it also manufactures pectin and hemicellulose in plant cells. Mitochondria are the power stations: a double membrane with the inner one folded into cristae that increase the surface area, carrying the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, and a fluid matrix holding enzymes of the citric acid cycle, sometimes with mitochondrial DNA; they carry out aerobic respiration and release energy from glucose as adenosine triphosphate, which is why muscle and gland cells are packed with them. Lysosomes are membrane sacs of hydrolytic enzymes at an acidic pH which digest worn organelles, engulfed bacteria and food particles; they are formed by the Golgi apparatus, and their enzymes are harmless as long as the membrane holds them in. The vacuole is a membrane-bound sac: large and permanent in plant cells where it stores sap and generates turgor pressure that holds the cell firm, and small and temporary in animal cells as food or contractile vacuoles, the latter pumping out excess water in protozoa. Peroxisomes carry oxidative enzymes, converting hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen, and breaking down fatty acids; centrosomes with their pair of centrioles organise the spindle at cell division and are found in animal cells; and the cytoskeleton, a network of microfilaments of actin, intermediate filaments and microtubules of tubulin, maintains cell shape, anchors organelles and drives movement of the cell and of materials inside it.

items: Nucleus: double envelope with pores, chromatin and nucleolus; directs the cell and assembles ribosomes.
Ribosomes: two subunits of RNA and protein, the site of translation in free and bound forms.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum: ribosome-studded, synthesises proteins for secretion, membrane or lysosomes.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: no ribosomes, makes lipids, stores calcium and detoxifies drugs.
Golgi apparatus: modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles; makes cell wall materials in plants.
Mitochondria: double membrane with cristae and matrix, carrying aerobic respiration and ATP production.
Lysosomes: digestive enzyme sacs that remove worn organelles and engulfed material.
Vacuoles: large central sap vacuole giving turgor in plants, small temporary vacuoles in animals.
Peroxisomes oxidise fatty acids and destroy hydrogen peroxide; centrosomes organise the spindle.
Cytoskeleton of microfilaments, intermediate filaments and microtubules gives shape and movement.

items.text: A pancreatic cell is full of Golgi
items.note: It secretes digestive enzymes continuously, so its rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus occupy much of the cytoplasm.

items.text: Why a muscle cell needs mitochondria
items.note: Contraction demands ATP at a high rate, so heart muscle cells are densely packed with mitochondria, each with many cristae.

blocks.text: The distinction between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells is the deepest in cell biology, and the comparison is almost always requested as a table. Prokaryotes — the bacteria and archaea — lack a membrane-bound nucleus, so their DNA lies free in a region called the nucleoid, usually as a single circular chromosome with additional small rings called plasmids; they lack membrane-bound organelles entirely, having no mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus or lysosomes. Their ribosomes are smaller, of the 70S type rather than the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm, which is the reason certain antibiotics can poison bacterial ribosomes without harming the patient’s cells. Their cell wall, when present, is made of peptidoglycan rather than cellulose or chitin, many carry a capsule as an outermost layer, and motility is by flagella of a different structure from those of eukaryotic cells. Eukaryotic cells, by contrast, hold their DNA inside a nuclear envelope bound to histone proteins in linear chromosomes, possess the full complement of membrane-bound organelles, have 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes as well as 70S ribosomes inside mitochondria and chloroplasts, and divide by mitosis rather than by binary fission. Their size is generally far greater, from about 10 micrometres upwards, while a bacterium is usually 1 to 5 micrometres. Both cell types share the essentials: a plasma membrane of lipid and protein, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA as the genetic material and the same genetic code in both, and ATP as the immediate energy currency. The comparison matters beyond classification because it explains the mechanism of antibiotics, the origin of eukaryotic organelles through endosymbiosis, and the practical limits of microscopes.

items: Prokaryotes have no nuclear envelope: DNA lies in a nucleoid, usually one circular chromosome plus plasmids.
Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles; mitochondria, ER, Golgi and lysosomes are absent.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 70S; eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S.
Bacterial walls are of peptidoglycan; eukaryotic walls, where present, are cellulose or chitin.
Prokaryotes divide by binary fission; eukaryotes divide by mitosis with a spindle.
Eukaryotic DNA is linear, bound to histones and enclosed in the nucleus.
Both share the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, DNA and ATP.
70S ribosomes also occur in eukaryotic mitochondria and chloroplasts, a hint of endosymbiotic origin.

items.note: Penicillin weakens the peptidoglycan wall that only bacteria build, and streptomycin jams the 70S ribosome — targets human cells do not have.
Mitochondria have their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes and divide by fission, which is the evidence for their origin as engulfed bacteria.

learn.title: The plasma membrane and transport across it

blocks.text: The plasma membrane is a fluid mosaic of phospholipids and proteins, and its structure explains everything it does. The phospholipids form a bilayer with their water-loving phosphate heads facing outwards into the aqueous surroundings and their water-fearing fatty acid tails tucked inside, so the interior is a hydrophobic barrier that polar molecules and ions cannot cross unaided. Cholesterol sits between the phospholipids in animal cells, restricting movement at low temperatures and preventing packing at high ones, which keeps the membrane fluid over a useful range. Proteins are scattered through the bilayer rather than coating its surface: integral proteins span the whole membrane as channels and carriers, while peripheral proteins sit on one face and often act as enzymes or anchors, and carbohydrate chains attached to proteins and lipids on the outer face form the glycocalyx, used for cell recognition. Transport across this barrier follows four mechanisms. Simple diffusion is the net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, continuing until the particles are evenly spread; it is passive, requiring no energy, and only small non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the lipid freely. Facilitated diffusion uses channel and carrier proteins to let polar molecules such as glucose and ions such as sodium and potassium pass down their gradient — still passive, since the energy comes from the gradient itself. Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane from higher water potential to lower water potential, and its consequence in plant cells is turgor: in a hypotonic solution water enters, the cell swells against the wall and becomes turgid; in an isotonic solution there is no net movement; in a hypertonic solution water leaves, the cell shrinks and plasmolysis occurs as the membrane pulls away from the wall. Active transport is the movement of substances against their concentration gradient, from lower to higher concentration, and it requires energy supplied directly by carrier proteins that hydrolyse ATP — the sodium-potassium pump, which expels three sodium ions for every two potassium ions it takes in, is the standard example, and it maintains the nerve impulse and cell volume. Bulk transport handles what cannot cross at all: exocytosis moves material out when a secretory vesicle fuses with the membrane and spills its contents, and endocytosis brings material in, either as phagocytosis of a solid particle, pinocytosis of dissolved material, or receptor-mediated endocytosis in which specific molecules bind a receptor before the membrane invaginates; both require energy and both change the shape of the membrane rather than opening a pore.

items: The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins — a fluid mosaic — with cholesterol fluidifying it.
Simple diffusion is passive, down the gradient, and limited to small non-polar molecules.
Facilitated diffusion uses channel and carrier proteins and is still passive because it follows the gradient.
Osmosis is the diffusion of water through a selectively permeable membrane from high to low water potential.
Hypotonic makes cells turgid, isotonic gives no net change, and hypertonic causes plasmolysis.
Active transport moves against the gradient using ATP-driven carriers, as in the sodium-potassium pump.
Exocytosis secretes by vesicle fusion; endocytosis imports by invagination, in phagocytic, pinocytic or receptor-mediated form.
All bulk transport and active transport require energy; diffusion and osmosis do not.

keyPoints: The cell theory states that all organisms are made of cells, the cell is the unit of life, and cells come only from cells.
Hooke named cells; Leeuwenhoek saw living ones; Schleiden and Schwann united the theory; Virchow completed it.
The nucleus stores DNA and the nucleolus makes ribosome subunits.
Rough ER makes proteins for export; smooth ER makes lipids and detoxifies.
The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages proteins into secretory vesicles.
Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration across cristae and matrix.
Lysosomes digest worn organelles and engulfed material with their enclosed enzymes.
The plant vacuole holds sap and generates the turgor that supports the cell.
Prokaryotes lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles and have 70S ribosomes.
The membrane is a phospholipid bilayer with embedded proteins and cholesterol for fluidity.
Diffusion and osmosis are passive; active transport and bulk transport require ATP.
Hypotonic makes cells turgid, isotonic leaves no net change and hypertonic causes plasmolysis.

questions.prompt: The organelle known as the powerhouse of the cell is the:
questions.explanation: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration and release energy as ATP.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly completes the cell theory?
options: All cells arise from pre-existing cells
Cells are formed from non-living matter
Only animal cells are true cells
questions.answer: All cells arise from pre-existing cells
questions.explanation: Virchow stated omne cellula e cellula, closing the theory against spontaneous generation.

questions.prompt: Movement of a substance against its concentration gradient requires:
questions.explanation: Active transport uses ATP-driven pumps to move solutes from lower to higher concentration.

questions.prompt: The organelle that digests worn-out organelles and bacteria is the:
questions.explanation: Lysosomes hold hydrolytic enzymes at acidic pH which break down engulfed material.

questions.prompt: The site of protein synthesis in the cell is the __________.
questions.explanation: Ribosomes read messenger RNA and assemble amino acids into a polypeptide.

questions.prompt: The region of a prokaryotic cell where the circular chromosome lies, without a nuclear envelope, is called the __________.
questions.explanation: Prokaryotic DNA lies free in the nucleoid rather than within a nucleus.

questions.prompt: State three differences between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell.
questions.answer: A prokaryotic cell has no membrane-bound nucleus, so its DNA lies free in a nucleoid region as a circular chromosome, whereas a eukaryotic cell holds its linear chromosomes inside a nuclear envelope. Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria, endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus, while eukaryotes possess them all. Their ribosomes also differ, since prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes and eukaryotic cytoplasm has 80S ribosomes, and prokaryotes divide by binary fission where eukaryotes divide by mitosis.
questions.explanation: Any three of: nucleus, membrane-bound organelles, ribosome size, DNA form and mode of division.

questions.prompt: What is meant by the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane?
questions.answer: The fluid mosaic model describes the membrane as a fluid phospholipid bilayer in which proteins are scattered like tiles in a mosaic rather than arranged in a rigid pattern. The phospholipids form the continuous double layer with their hydrophilic heads facing the aqueous fluids outside and inside and their hydrophobic tails inward, and they move laterally within their own layer, which gives the membrane its fluidity. Proteins are of two kinds: integral proteins that extend through the bilayer as channels and carriers, and peripheral proteins attached to one surface as enzymes or anchors. Cholesterol within the bilayer in animal cells adjusts the fluidity by preventing tight packing at high temperatures and restricting movement at low ones, so the membrane remains functional across a range of temperatures.
questions.explanation: Bilayer with heads and tails, lateral movement giving fluidity, the two classes of protein, and the role of cholesterol.

questions.answer: Diffusion is the net movement of particles of any substance from a region where they are more concentrated to one where they are less concentrated, continuing until they are evenly distributed; it is passive, requires no energy and depends on the concentration gradient. Osmosis is a special case in which only water moves, and it does so through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to one of lower water potential. The distinction matters because osmosis depends on the membrane and on water potential specifically, whereas diffusion can occur without any membrane at all.
questions.explanation: Diffusion as general movement of particles down a gradient; osmosis as water through a membrane down a potential gradient.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the mitochondrion and explain how it is adapted for aerobic respiration.
questions.answer: The mitochondrion is a double-membraned organelle of about one micrometre in length. The outer membrane is smooth and freely permeable to small molecules, while the inner membrane is folded into numerous shelves called cristae, which project into the interior and increase the surface area available for the reactions of the electron transport chain and for the ATP synthase enzymes embedded in it. The inner membrane is impermeable to most molecules, so a proton gradient can be built across it, and the energy of that gradient drives ATP synthesis as protons return through ATP synthase. Between the two membranes lies the intermembrane space into which the protons are pumped. The cavity enclosed by the inner membrane contains the matrix, a dense fluid holding the enzymes of the citric acid cycle, small circular mitochondrial DNA, 70S ribosomes and granules, so the mitochondrion can make some of its own proteins and divide independently. The combination of cristae for surface area, an enclosed gradient, and matrix enzymes for the citric acid cycle makes the mitochondrion the site where the energy of food is converted into ATP, which is why cells with high energy demands such as muscle fibres and sperm tails contain very many of them.
questions.explanation: Double membrane, cristae and surface area, the proton gradient and ATP synthase, the matrix with its enzymes, and the link to energy demand.

questions.prompt: A plant cell is placed in a concentrated sugar solution. Describe what happens and explain the mechanism, then state what would be seen if it were returned to pure water.
questions.answer: The concentrated sugar solution is hypertonic to the cell sap, so its water potential outside is lower than that inside the cell. Water therefore leaves the cell by osmosis, moving through the selectively permeable plasma membrane from higher to lower water potential. As water is lost first from the cytoplasm and then from the large central vacuole, the volume of the protoplast falls and the membrane pulls away from the rigid cell wall, leaving a visible gap between wall and protoplast — the condition is called plasmolysis, and at first it is incipient as the corners begin to retract, then complete as the whole protoplast shrinks. The cell loses turgor and the plant tissue wilts. If the cell is returned to pure water, which is hypotonic, water re-enters by osmosis, the vacuole swells and the protoplast presses back against the wall; the wall resists further expansion, so the cell becomes turgid rather than bursting, and the process of recovery is called deplasmolysis. The cell wall is what prevents lysis in a hypotonic medium, an advantage animal cells do not have.
questions.explanation: Solution type and water potential, the direction of water movement, plasmolysis with the membrane pulling away, then deplasmolysis and turgor on return, with the wall preventing bursting.

questions.prompt: Explain why lysosomes are sometimes called suicide bags, and describe how the cell normally keeps them harmless.
questions.answer: Lysosomes are called suicide bags because they contain a powerful suite of hydrolytic enzymes — proteases, lipases, nucleases and carbohydrases — capable of digesting every major class of biological molecule. If the lysosomal membrane were to rupture while the cell were still healthy, those enzymes would be released into the cytoplasm and would digest the cell itself, killing it from within; controlled rupture of lysosomes does in fact occur during programmed cell death, which is why the name has persisted. The cell keeps them harmless in three ways. The enzymes are synthesised in the rough endoplasmic reticulum and packaged by the Golgi apparatus into a membrane-bound vesicle, so they never lie free in the cytoplasm. The membrane carries proteins that pump protons in to maintain the acidic pH near five, which is the pH at which the enzymes work — at the neutral pH of the cytoplasm they are almost inactive, so a small leak does little damage. And the lysosome membrane itself is heavily glycosylated on its inner surface, which protects it from attack by its own enzymes. The result is a compartmentalised digestion system that recycles worn organelles and destroys bacteria without endangering the cell.
questions.explanation: The enzymes and their danger, then the three protections: membrane enclosure, acidic pH inactivating them at cytoplasmic pH, and the glycosylated inner surface.
